title: ECS services and load balancers
idea: An ECS service keeps a set number of tasks running and registers each in a target group: the tasks a load balancer may send requests to.
points: `desiredCount` is how many tasks to keep running; ECS replaces any that stop.
A listener, the load balancer's open port, forwards requests to a target group.
The service's `loadBalancers` entry names the target group, container and container port.
The target group's health check decides which tasks get requests.

steps.caption: The service starts two tasks, its `desiredCount`, from one task definition.
Each new task is registered in the target group. The balancer health-checks it before sending requests.
Both tasks answer 200, so both are healthy. Client requests now spread across them.
Task 2 starts failing its health checks. The balancer stops sending it requests.
ECS stops the unhealthy task. The service is below its desired count, so it starts a replacement.
The replacement passes its health check and joins the rotation. The count is 2 again.

pitfalls: Create the target group with type `ip`; `instance`, the default, is wrong for `awsvpc` tasks.
Match `containerName` and `containerPort` to the task definition; they must exist there.
Set `healthCheckGracePeriodSeconds` for slow-starting apps; the default is 0.

quiz.q: A task fails its target group health check. What happens?
options: Nothing changes until you restart the service
The whole service stops until you fix it
The load balancer restarts the container itself
The balancer routes around it and ECS replaces it
quiz.why: A target group routes only to healthy targets. ECS stops tasks that fail load balancer health checks and starts new ones to match `desiredCount`.

takeaway: Desired count keeps tasks alive; health checks decide which ones get traffic.
